paper.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
paper.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.

paper.title: L2C2: Enhancing Large-scale Chiplets for Agent Long-Context LLM Inference with Sparse and Distributed Attention
paper.abstract: Long-context inference is a rising demand for LLMs, especially for agent applications. Sparse attention (SpAt) and chiplet technology are promising solutions to reduce computations and scale hardware performance. However, deploying SpAt on distributed chiplets necessitates context parallelism for workload partitioning, introducing complex distributed attention. In this work, we present L2C2, a system optimization for distributed SpAt in long-context inference. During the partial-prefill stage, we propose a novel Split-Comm Attention mechanism that leverages the high-bandwidth interconnect of chiplets to trade communication overhead for reduced memory access. We combine it with conventional Ring Attention to form a Bi-Mode method that adapts to varying input sequence lengths. During the decoding stage, we analyze the cause of memory access imbalance and address it by static interleaved token assignment. Dynamic agile cache balancing is also proposed to adapt to SpAt skewness. Evaluations show our optimization can achieve 1.45$\times$ and 1.53$\times$ speedup in partial-prefill and decoding with SpAt on large-scale chiplets.

paper.title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
paper.abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.

paper.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
paper.abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD

paper.title: MixMoMo: Accelerating Extra--Large MoE Inference with Mixed--Precision GPU--NPU Execution on Mobile Devices
paper.abstract: Mobile agents and on-device intelligence increasingly demand more capable models on smartphones. Through sparse expert activation, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity, yet growing numbers of fine-grained experts complicate loading and computation. Model compression complements expert offloading by reducing storage and computation costs. Among compression techniques, mixed-precision quantization assigns lower expert bitwidths to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, existing offline metrics and routing scores fail to reflect expert quantization sensitivity, undermining precision assignment. Diverse bitwidths also complicate balanced expert allocation across GPUs and NPUs with distinct execution characteristics, while tile-wise dequantization underutilizes NPU vector parallelism. We present MixMoMo, an efficient mixed-precision inference runtime for extra-large MoE models on heterogeneous mobile SoCs. MixMoMo combines offline quantization-impact profiles with activation-based runtime risk estimates for quality-constrained expert bitwidth assignment. It further adopts precision-structured execution for balanced GPU-NPU expert allocation and HVX-parallel dequantization for efficient NPU vector utilization. Across three MoE models and five benchmarks on two mobile platforms, MixMoMo achieves average decoding speedups of 3.72x over uniform Q4_0 and 1.53x over the strongest mixed-precision MoE baseline.

paper.title: Asymmetric Speculative Decoding: Unlocking In-Context Learning in Draft Models
paper.abstract: Speculative decoding addresses Large Language Model (LLM) inference latency by first drafting and then verifying in parallel. Yet practical speedups fall far short of theoretical bounds, especially on reasoning tasks. We identify the root cause as task isomorphism: existing methods provide identical prompts to both models, forcing the draft model to solve problems beyond its capacity. This produces high rejection rates that eliminate parallelization gains. We discover that acceptance rates increase monotonically during generation, revealing a latent in-context learning (ICL) effect wherein the draft model progressively aligns with the target distribution by learning from verified tokens. Controlled experiments with varying context window sizes confirm this improvement stems from ICL-driven alignment rather than token difficulty. Motivated by this finding, we propose Asymmetric Speculative Decoding (AsymSpec), a training-free framework that decouples the prompts provided to draft and target models. By supplying the draft model with task-relevant example solutions, we reformulate its objective from reasoning to simulation, amplifying the ICL effect from the first token. We prove AsymSpec produces exact samples and converges exponentially to the target distribution. Across reasoning, code generation, and summarization tasks, AsymSpec achieves 2.29$\times$ to 4.95$\times$ speedup over autoregressive decoding, outperforming standard speculative decoding without model retraining.

paper.title: Strong Starts, Simple Recipes: Unified Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation from Multimodal Specialists
paper.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates separately trained domain specialists into a single unified model. Existing methods focus on refining the distillation procedure while initializing the student from a base model or a multi-domain SFT checkpoint, which leaves capability integration largely to distillation itself. Instead, we treat the starting point as a design variable and propose Unified MOPD (Uni-MOPD), which pairs a strong start with a simple recipe: a training-free uniform merge of specialists from the same base model initializes the student, and short MOPD with uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL refines it. Across five multimodal domains and 19 benchmarks, our study establishes three findings. (1) The starting point matters more than subsequent training choices: before any training, the uniform merge already matches the score that the base model reaches after 200 MOPD updates, and after short distillation it matches higher-scoring, search-based starts. (2) Short MOPD recovers most of the capabilities the merge leaves unintegrated; it improves every domain, with the largest gains where the domain teacher still leads. (3) From a strong start, uniform domain sampling and full-vocabulary reverse KL match or exceed every evaluated sampling strategy and divergence, without schedules, per-token weighting, or truncation hyperparameters. Uni-MOPD outperforms Open-MOPD at the same training budget while training 3.3 times faster than its released code. We will release the training framework, specialist checkpoints, and unified student.

paper.title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
paper.abstract: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.

paper.title: PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving
paper.abstract: Pipeline parallelism can serve long-context language models on PCIe servers and across heterogeneous GPU clusters. Existing engines split prefill into token chunks to limit decode stalls. The chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload model weights more often. Large chunks can keep the GPU and the link busy long enough to delay interactive requests. PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can run between slices. A fused Triton Hadamard-INT4 codec compresses activations, which travel in independently sized row groups over parallel TCP sockets. The scheduler uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. We evaluated PipeAxes in 97 replays covering 5,016 requests on A800, RTX 4090, and RTX 3090 GPUs. All 74 requests met their latency targets during a tenfold bandwidth swing. In a four-stage mixture-of-experts pipeline, PipeAxes served requests within their latency targets at 23.3x the rate of calibrated Revisit-PP and 4.44x the rate of Fixed-4096 with Express. In a mixed 64K-context workload, p95 time to first token for short requests fell from 129.8 s with native vLLM to 512 ms. With INT4 transport, MMLU accuracy rose by 0.06 percentage points and GSM8K accuracy fell by 0.46 percentage points relative to BF16.

paper.title: A Differential Computing Accelerator for LLM Inference Leveraging Bit-Slice Transition Sparsity
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become foundational to modern artificial intelligence. Driven by scaling laws, their rapid growth poses increasing computational and memory challenges for deployment. To accelerate the general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations that dominate LLM computation, bit-slice architectures decompose quantized operands along the bit dimension, exposing slice-level sparsity and redundancy. However, existing bit-slice designs primarily exploit sparsity in high-order slices, while dense low-order slices still offer substantial untapped reuse opportunities. We observe that bit-slice vectors (BSVs) are highly clustered in Hamming space, with many BSVs lying only a few bit flips away from a small set of representative patterns. Based on this observation, we propose ISTS, an algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator that leverages representative BSV patterns as shared Steiner points to reuse partial sums across slices, substantially reducing computation. Specifically, the partial sum of each target BSV can be reconstructed from that of its assigned Steiner point using only a few additions or subtractions. On the algorithmic side, we propose Steiner Absorption Table Construction (SATC), which selects a compact set of Steiner points to absorb BSVs with only a few bidirectional bit flips, while FlipPrune selectively prunes flips to further expand the reusable BSV population. On the hardware side, we design a lightweight accelerator that supports Steiner reuse for static linear layer weights and runtime-generated attention K/V tensors. Comprehensive evaluations show that ISTS achieves average speedups of $3.09\times$, $2.41\times$, $2.18\times$, $1.27\times$, and $1.41\times$ over the state-of-the-art accelerators ANT, BBS, LUT Tensor Core, Transitive Array, and MCBP-BRCR, respectively.
